questions.stem: When a gas is heated in a sealed container, its pressure increases. Which statement best explains this using the kinetic particle model?

options.text: The particles expand and take up more space
The particles move faster, colliding with the walls more frequently and with greater force
More particles are created by the heating
The particles get heavier when heated

questions.explanation: Heating increases the kinetic energy of gas particles, making them move faster. Faster particles hit the container walls more often and with greater force, increasing pressure. Particles do not expand, get heavier, or multiply when heated. It is the speed and frequency of collisions that change, not the particles themselves.

questions.stem: A drop of food colouring is placed in cold water and in hot water. The colour spreads faster in hot water. Why?

options.text: Hot water has fewer particles, leaving more gaps
The food colouring dissolves but does not diffuse
Particles in hot water move faster, so diffusion happens more quickly
The food colouring is lighter in hot water

questions.explanation: In hot water, water particles have more kinetic energy and move faster. They collide with the food colouring particles more frequently and with greater energy, causing the dye particles to spread (diffuse) more quickly. Hot water does not have fewer particles, and the mass of the dye does not change with temperature.

questions.stem: According to the kinetic particle model, what is temperature a measure of?

options.text: The total energy of all particles in a substance
The average kinetic energy of the particles
The number of particles in a substance
The size of the particles

questions.explanation: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. It is not the total energy (that would be internal energy) and does not depend on the number or size of particles. A cup of tea can be hotter than a swimming pool even though the pool has more total thermal energy.

questions.stem: A student claims that particles in a solid are completely still. Is this correct?

options.text: Yes, solid particles cannot move at all
Yes, only liquid and gas particles move
No, particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions
No, particles in a solid move freely like in a gas

questions.explanation: Particles in a solid are not still; they vibrate about fixed positions. They have kinetic energy but cannot move from place to place because strong forces hold them in a regular arrangement. Only at absolute zero (0 K) would particles theoretically have zero kinetic energy. They do not move freely like gas particles.

questions.stem: Two containers hold the same gas at the same temperature. Container A has double the volume of Container B. Which container has the higher gas pressure?

options.text: Container A, because it has more space for particles to move
Container B, because the same number of particles in a smaller volume means more frequent collisions with the walls
Both have the same pressure because the temperature is the same
Cannot determine without knowing the mass of gas

questions.explanation: We cannot determine the pressure without knowing how much gas is in each container. If both contain the same amount of gas, Container B would have higher pressure (same particles in less volume = more collisions per unit area). But the question only states same gas and same temperature, not the same amount. The amount of gas (number of particles) is essential information.
